forces: Two treble instruments and continuo; here violin, flute, viola da gamba and keyboard
performers: New Comma Baroque: Matthew C. Cataldi, Baroque violin; Leighann Daihl, Baroque flute; Phillip W. Serna, viola da gamba; Emily J. Morlan, historical keyboards
intro: The Sonade opens La Piémontaise, from Couperin’s Les Nations, and is written in three parts, with violin and flute playing long notes, quick runs and short airs over the bass. New Comma Baroque performs it with four players, as viola da gamba and keyboard share the bass line.

sections.label: A · Long notes, Gravement
sections.mNote: Violin and flute overlap above the shared bass.

sections.label: B · Vivement, upper parts and bass
sections.mNote: Runs pass between the upper parts and the bass.

sections.label: C · Gravement, with even notes
sections.mNote: The upper parts hold long notes while the bass moves.

sections.label: D · Vivement et marqué
sections.mNote: Quick figures with clearly marked beginnings.

sections.label: E · Two airs, major and minor
sections.mNote: A major-key air returns after a second air in the minor.

sections.label: F · Gravement et marqué
sections.mNote: Dotted figures above a held bass.

sections.label: G · Légèrement, in six-eight
sections.mNote: Running quavers pass through all three parts.

relations.label: The first air returns
relations.basis: Inside the paired airs, the opening major-mode material returns after the minor-mode contrast. This agrees with the air at 274 s and the return to major described by the listening note near 450 s. CENS diagonal mean 0.966, sustained 37 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 158 s (cache/form/couperin-nations-piemontaise.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Scoring and opening Gravement
cues.text: Violin and flute take the two upper parts; gamba and keyboard share the bass. In the opening Gravement, one upper voice often holds a note while the other moves. Trills decorate the long notes, and the bass has its own ornaments.
cues.evidence: Couperin, La Piémontoise, Cmaj7 edition (2022), score pp. 1–2. Performers are identified in the recording’s Commons description. Score: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/25/IMSLP779316-PMLP297657-Couperin_-_La_Pi%C3%A9montoise.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Death of Charles Couperin, 1679
cues.text: Couperin’s father Charles, organist of Saint-Gervais in Paris, died in 1679, and the post was held in reserve for the boy. Lalande filled the organ bench until François took it himself in 1685.
cues.evidence: Opéra Royal de Versailles, biography of Couperin: Charles’s death in 1679, François titular by survivance, Lalande’s interim. Larousse, Dictionnaire de la musique: François in the post from 1685. https://www.operaroyal-versailles.fr/genre-event/couperin/ and https://www.larousse.fr/encyclopedie/musdico/Fran%C3%A7ois_Couperin/167027

cues.title: Bass semiquavers, first Vivement
cues.text: The Vivement gives running semiquavers to the bass as well as to the upper parts. A phrase can begin below the violin and flute and rise into their register. The keyboard and gamba have substantial material together.
cues.evidence: Score, first Vivement, bars 30 onwards, pp. 3–5. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/25/IMSLP779316-PMLP297657-Couperin_-_La_Pi%C3%A9montoise.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Couperin’s preface, 1726
cues.text: In his 1726 preface, Couperin told a story about his first sonata. He presented it as the work of an Italian composer whose name was an anagram of his own, and it was well received. He then wrote more sonatas under the same disguise.
cues.evidence: Couperin’s preface to Les Nations (1726), discussed by Brian Robins, 22 July 2019. https://earlymusicreview.com/francois-couperin-les-nations-1726/

cues.title: Royal chapel organist, 1693
cues.text: Couperin’s teacher Thomelin, organist of the royal chapel, died in 1693. Couperin won the competition for the post and served the January quarter of each year. He remained an organist of the royal chapel for the rest of his working life.
cues.evidence: Larousse, Dictionnaire de la musique: after Thomelin’s death in 1693 he won the royal chapel organist’s post “par concours” for the January quarter. https://www.larousse.fr/encyclopedie/musdico/Fran%C3%A7ois_Couperin/167027. Opéra Royal de Versailles gives the same appointment: https://www.operaroyal-versailles.fr/genre-event/couperin/

cues.title: First air, violin solo
cues.text: The first air is in G major and marked Gracieusement. The violin plays the opening phrase above the bass in bars 1–7 while the flute rests, and the bass moves in small steps with ornaments. Then the flute takes up the tune and the violin rests.
cues.evidence: Score, first Air, pp. 12–13: first dessus alone above the bass in bars 1–7, second dessus enters in bar 8. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/25/IMSLP779316-PMLP297657-Couperin_-_La_Pi%C3%A9montoise.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The four ordres of Les Nations
cues.text: The four ordres of Les Nations are named after France, Spain, the Empire and Piedmont. Each opens with a sonata in the Italian style, followed by French dances. In this ordre the printed score follows the sonata with an allemande marked “nobly, and without slowness”.
cues.evidence: Collection and design: https://earlymusicreview.com/francois-couperin-les-nations-1726/. Allemande marking, ‘Noblement, et sans lenteur’, score p. 20: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/25/IMSLP779316-PMLP297657-Couperin_-_La_Pi%C3%A9montoise.pdf. English translation is literal.

cues.title: L’Art de toucher le clavecin, 1716
cues.text: In L’Art de toucher le clavecin (1716) Couperin recommended putting a mirror on the music desk to cure a pupil’s grimaces. With small children he took the key of the harpsichord home, so that nothing he had spent three quarters of an hour setting right would be undone while he was away.
cues.evidence: Couperin, L’Art de toucher le clavecin (1716), opening instructions on grimaces, the mirror and “la clef de l’instrument” (Nicolas Sceaux’s transcription, p. 2–3): https://musebaroque.fr/archives/Partitions/Couperin_clavecin2.pdf

cues.title: Preface to Les Nations, 1726
cues.text: In his preface to Les Nations (1726), Couperin named both Corelli and Lully, “both of whose compositions I shall love as long as I live”. The book contains Italian sonatas and French dances.
cues.evidence: Couperin, preface to Les Nations (1726), in the English translation quoted by Brian Robins. https://earlymusicreview.com/francois-couperin-les-nations-1726/

cues.title: Opening of the Gravement et marqué
cues.text: The later Gravement et marqué begins with a long C in the bass. The violin plays a dotted figure, and the flute enters with it a bar later.
cues.evidence: Score, Gravement et marqué, p. 16, opening three bars: held C in the bass and successive entries of the upper parts. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/25/IMSLP779316-PMLP297657-Couperin_-_La_Pi%C3%A9montoise.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Final Légèrement in six-eight
cues.text: The final Légèrement is in six-eight. The flute begins the running quavers while the violin rests, and the figures soon pass between the upper parts and the bass. The three lines continue to exchange them until the end of the sonata.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The bass breaks into running notes
transitions.to: B · Vivement, upper parts and bass
transitions.how: A D major chord closes the slow opening. Vivement begins in G minor and common time. The violin drops out after its first note while flute and bass continue. Running semiquavers soon pass between the gamba, keyboard and upper instruments.
transitions.evidence: Score, bars 29–33, p. 3: D major closing chord and Vivement in common time. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/25/IMSLP779316-PMLP297657-Couperin_-_La_Pi%C3%A9montoise.pdf

transitions.title: E♭ under the held notes
transitions.from: B · Vivement, upper parts and bass
transitions.how: The new Gravement opens on E♭ major, with E♭ in the bass and G and B♭ in the upper parts. The metre returns to three-two, and violin and flute hold long notes. Later Couperin asks for notes égales, evenly played notes, as the gamba and keyboard bass begin to move beneath them.

transitions.title: Into the Air in G major
transitions.to: E · Two airs, major and minor
transitions.how: The quick movement slows to très lentement and closes on D major. The air follows in G major, in triple metre, with G in the bass. Marked Gracieusement, it opens with the violin playing a rounded, ornamented phrase over gamba and keyboard. The flute rests at first and enters later for its own turn.
transitions.evidence: Score, final bars of Vivement et marqué and opening of the Air, pp. 11–12. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/25/IMSLP779316-PMLP297657-Couperin_-_La_Pi%C3%A9montoise.pdf

transitions.title: From dotted notes to six-eight
transitions.how: The slow section ends in D major, and Légèrement begins over G in the bass. The metre changes from common time to six-eight. The flute starts a run of continuous quavers. The violin plays a single note and then rests. Under the first phrase the gamba and keyboard hold dotted crotchets, and after that they join the faster movement.
transitions.evidence: Score, join between Gravement et marqué and Légèrement, p. 17. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/25/IMSLP779316-PMLP297657-Couperin_-_La_Pi%C3%A9montoise.pdf

composer.epithet: Musician who played for Louis XIV on Sundays, known at the harpsichord for held notes, trills and well-placed silences.
facts: Son of Charles Couperin; nephew of Louis; organist at Saint-Gervais from 1685
Royal chapel organist from 1693; chamber harpsichordist from 1717
Four books, 1713–30: 27 ordres; L’Art de toucher le clavecin, 1716–17
Two organ masses; Leçons de Ténèbres; chamber concerts and viol suites
composer.background:
On Sundays in 1714 and 1715, François Couperin played chamber music for the ageing Louis XIV. The violinist François Duval joined him, with wind players and a viol; Couperin played the harpsichord. When he published the Concerts royaux in 1722, he recalled that the king had summoned him “almost every Sunday of the year”. The dances in the collection, among them an allemande, a grave sarabande and a little chaconne, had been played in the king’s rooms. Louis XIV had once danced in his own court ballets.

Couperin was born in Paris in 1668, into a family already established at the organ of Saint-Gervais. His uncle Louis had held the post before his father Charles, and had died before François was born. When Charles died in 1679, the church kept the succession open for the boy, and Michel-Richard de Lalande covered the duties until he was ready. François studied with Jacques Thomelin and took over in 1685. At twenty-five he won one of the four organists’ places at the royal chapel. He kept his Paris work, travelled to court for his quarter of service and taught the royal children.
